text: Six days later Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother and led them up a high mountain by themselves.
There he was transfigured before them: his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as the light.
And suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him.
Peter spoke up and said to Jesus, "Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, I will put up three shelters here—one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah."
While he was still speaking, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him!"
When the disciples heard it, they fell face down, terrified.
But Jesus came and touched them. "Get up," he said. "Do not be afraid."
And when they looked up, they saw no one but Jesus alone.
As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus ordered them, "Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead."
The disciples asked him, "Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?"
He answered, "Elijah does come, and he will restore all things.
But I tell you, Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him; instead they did to him whatever they pleased. In the same way the Son of Man is about to suffer at their hands."
Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them about John the Baptist.
When they came to the crowd, a man approached him, knelt before him,
and said, "Lord, have mercy on my son. He has seizures and suffers terribly; he often falls into the fire and often into the water.
I brought him to your disciples, but they could not heal him."
Jesus answered, "You unbelieving and perverse generation! How long must I be with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring him here to me."
Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed from that moment.
Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and asked, "Why couldn't we drive it out?"

versions.text: Later the disciples came to Jesus privately and asked, "Why couldn't we drive it out?"
versions.explanation: Τότε means "then" (at that point in the sequence), not "later," which implies a vaguer and longer interval. "Then" also keeps the narrative rhythm consistent with verse 13, where the same word is rendered "Then."

text: He told them, "Because your faith is so small. Truly I tell you, if you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move; nothing will be impossible for you."
"But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting."

versions.text: But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting.
versions.explanation: Verse 20 closes Jesus' speech with a closing quotation mark, yet verse 21 continues his words with no quotation marks at all. The punctuation must be consistent: either remove the closing quotation mark at the end of verse 20 and place it here, or mark verse 21 as direct speech as suggested. As it stands, an oral reader cannot tell that verse 21 is still Jesus speaking. A footnote noting that this sentence is absent from the earliest manuscripts would also help the reader.

text: As they were gathering together in Galilee, Jesus said to them, "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into human hands.
They will kill him, and on the third day he will be raised." And they were deeply grieved.
When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the temple tax came to Peter and asked, "Doesn't your teacher pay the temple tax?"
"Yes," he said. And when he went into the house, Jesus spoke first: "What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect duties and taxes—from their own sons, or from others?"
"From others," he replied. Jesus said to him, "Then the sons are exempt.
But so that we do not offend them, go to the sea, throw out a hook, and take the first fish you catch. Open its mouth and you will find a coin. Take it and give it to them for me and for you.

versions.text: But so that we do not give offense, go to the sea, throw out a hook, and take the first fish you catch. Open its mouth and you will find a coin. Take it and give it to them for me and for you."
versions.explanation: The object αὐτούς ("them," i.e. the tax collectors) is dropped in the current rendering, leaving "give offense" vague; restoring "them" ties the sentence to the collectors mentioned in verse 24 and reads more naturally aloud. Consider also a footnote on "a coin": the Greek stater was worth four drachmas—exactly the temple tax for two people.
